title: Optimized plasma-assisted bi-layer photoresist fabrication protocol for high resolution microfabrication of thin-film metal electrodes on porous polymer membranes
author: Schuller, Rothbauer, et al.

steps.title: Prepare PVA solution
steps.instruction: Dissolve 4 g polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) in 100 ml deionized water, stir at 70 °C (covered with aluminum foil) until fully dissolved, filter through a 22 µm syringe filter, and let the solution cool to room temperature.

steps.title: Clean and pre‑heat glass carrier
steps.instruction: Clean a Schott D263T eco glass substrate sequentially with acetone and isopropyl alcohol, then place it on a hot plate set to 100 °C to evaporate any remaining solvent.

steps.title: O₂ plasma activation of glass
steps.instruction: Treat the cleaned glass with O₂ plasma at 300 W, 0.7 Torr for 45 seconds to improve PVA spreading.

steps.title: Spin‑coat PVA release layer
steps.instruction: Transfer the plasma‑treated glass to a spin coater, dispense the PVA solution with a pipette or syringe, and spin at 800 rpm for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Attach PET membrane to wet PVA
steps.instruction: Place a pre‑cut PET membrane (slightly larger than the glass) onto the still‑wet PVA layer, bending gently if needed to avoid wrinkles.

steps.title: Dry PVA with membrane attached
steps.instruction: Put the sample on a hot plate and ramp the temperature to 150 °C (the LOR3A bake temperature). If a ramping function is unavailable, bake sequentially at 70 °C, 100 °C, 120 °C, and 150 °C for 180 seconds each. Avoid rapid heating to prevent water‑induced wrinkles.

steps.title: Trim excess membrane
steps.instruction: After the sample cools to room temperature, cut away membrane portions that overlap the glass using a scalpel.

steps.title: Spin‑coat LOR3A release layer
steps.instruction: Spin LOR3A resist at 1000 rpm for 30 seconds, then soft‑bake at 150 °C for 180 seconds (temperature can be ramped or applied gradually as described in the previous drying step).

steps.title: Spin‑coat AZ5214E photoresist
steps.instruction: Spin AZ5214E (or a simple negative resist) at 3000 rpm for 30 seconds and soft‑bake at 100 °C for 30 seconds.

steps.title: UV expose electrode pattern
steps.instruction: Expose the sample through the photomask using 365 nm UV light with a dose of 40 mJ cm⁻².

steps.title: Post‑exposure bake and flood expose
steps.instruction: Bake the exposed sample at 120 °C for 70 seconds, then perform a flood exposure (no mask) with a dose of 240 mJ cm⁻².

steps.title: Develop resist
steps.instruction: Develop the sample in AZ726MIF (TMAH‑based developer) for 120 seconds, then rinse thoroughly with deionized water. (Typical AZ5214E development is 60 seconds; the extended time allows TMAH to dissolve LOR3A and create an undercut.)

steps.title: Dry samples
steps.instruction: Dry the developed samples using a nitrogen spray gun or leave them overnight in a desiccator.

steps.title: Argon plasma pretreatment
steps.instruction: Expose the samples to Ar plasma at 50 W RF power, 10 sccm Ar flow, for 60 seconds (using a plasma asher or RIE).

steps.title: Deposit gold layer
steps.instruction: Sputter approximately 80 nm of gold at 25 W in two 60‑second sputter cycles; maintain a base pressure of 2 × 10⁻⁵ mbar and a working pressure of 8 × 10⁻³ mbar. Do not exceed 25 W to avoid membrane overheating or metal spalling. Evaporation may be used as an alternative deposition method.

steps.title: Lift‑off and resist removal
steps.instruction: Soak the samples in N‑methyl‑pyrrolidone or N‑ethyl‑pyrrolidone for 10 minutes and sonicate at low power to remove the photoresist and any non‑patterned gold.

steps.title: Release membrane from carrier
steps.instruction: Soak the sample in deionized water for 1 minute, then gently pull the PET membrane off the glass carrier with tweezers.

steps.title: Optional notes for other metals
steps.instruction: For chromium adhesion, O₂ plasma improves bonding. If using PET membranes from other suppliers, plasma parameters may need adjustment. When sputtering metal combinations, keep power low to avoid spalling or cracking.

description: Several process parameters such as plasma power, type, duration and etc. were constantly evaluated, resulting in the optimized protocol presented above. Overall process parameters and results are summarized in Table 1. The gold microstructures fabricated on porous membranes achieved a resolution down to 2.5 μm. Fig. 2 shows a comparison of four parameter sets, Fig. 2A and B show thin-film microelectrodes fabricated using single-layer resist lift-off. The PET substrate in Fig. 2A was subjected to an O2 plasma before Au deposition, while the substrate in Fig. 2B was subjected to an Ar plasma both with a power of 50 W and an oxygen flow rate of 10 sccm. Fig. 2C and D shows microelectrodes fabricated using a bi-layer resist fabrication approach, both substrates were subjected to Ar plasma with a power of 50 W. In case of the sample in Fig. 2C the Ar flow rate was 20 sccm while the flow rate in Fig. 2D was 10 sccm, resulting in better adhesion of Au to the substrate. Also, O2 plasma at 10 sccm and 50 W could achieve results comparable to the best Ar treated samples down to a resolution of 2.5 μm only in the presence of a 5 nm chromium adhesion layer. As shown also in Table 1, any fabrication approaches that used only a single photoresist were inferior in terms of resolution to the optimized bi-layer photoresist fabrication methods. Also evident is the influence of high plasma and metal deposition powers resulting in structural and functional artifacts including thin-film delamination or cracking/ spalling of the metal layer. The improved performance of the presented optimized bi-layer lift-off fabrication protocol is not caused by physical etching known to increase surface area. For instance, Fig. 3 shows that plasma-treated PET membranes display similar surface roughness, thus area, in comparison to pristine non-modified samples.
